nameStory: Tree lungwort gets its name from its resemblance to lung tissue - if you look closely at its surface, you'll see a network of ridges and valleys that look remarkably like the inside of lungs! This resemblance was so striking to early botanists that they gave it multiple lung-related names, including 'oak lungs' and 'lung lichen.'
description: Tree lungwort is one of New England's most impressive lichens, forming large leafy patches that can grow as big as dinner plates on tree trunks. This foliose (leaf-like) lichen has a distinctive wrinkled, lung-like surface with a network of raised ridges and sunken valleys. When dry, it appears grayish-green to brownish, but transforms to a vibrant bright green when wet. It's actually a three-way partnership between a fungus, green algae, and cyanobacteria - a unique biological collaboration.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: The surface feels like soft leather and has deep ridges and valleys that create a brain-like or lung-like pattern - run your finger gently across it and you'll feel the distinct bumpy texture

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Large and impressive, often growing 4-8 inches across or even bigger - one of the largest leaf-like lichens you'll encounter in New England

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dramatic color change from dull gray-brown when dry to brilliant emerald green when wet - splash some water on it to see the transformation

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Loosely attached to bark with irregular, raggedy edges that often curl and overlap like old parchment

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Almost exclusively found on the bark of older deciduous trees, especially maples, birches, and oaks in undisturbed forests

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Look for tiny cup-shaped structures (soredia) along the ridges that feel slightly powdery when touched gently

habitat: Tree lungwort thrives in old-growth or mature forests with clean air, typically on the bark of large deciduous trees like sugar maples, birches, and oaks. You'll find it in cool, humid forest environments, often in ravines or north-facing slopes where moisture lingers. It's becoming increasingly rare in developed areas due to air pollution sensitivity.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant as spring rains wet the surface, showing off its bright green color transformation. This is an excellent time to observe the dramatic wet-to-dry color changes.
seasonality.summer: Often appears dull and grayish-brown during dry periods, but summer thunderstorms will bring out the brilliant green coloration. Growth is most active during humid summer months.
seasonality.fall: Remains visible but may be partially obscured by falling leaves. The cooler, damper weather brings out richer colors and makes the texture more pliable to touch.
seasonality.winter: Easily spotted against snow-covered bark, appearing as large grayish patches. Winter moisture from snow and ice keeps it hydrated and relatively green-tinted.

funFact: Tree lungwort is actually three different life forms living as one - it's not just a fungus and algae partnership like most lichens, but includes cyanobacteria as a third partner, making it one of nature's most complex cooperative relationships involving three different kingdoms of life!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other large foliose lichens, but none have tree lungwort's distinctive brain-like ridged surface texture. Remember: if it feels smooth, it's not lungwort - the bumpy, ridged texture is unmistakable once you know what to feel for.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name containing 'lungwort,' this lichen is completely unrelated to the flowering plant called lungwort (Pulmonaria species). The name similarity comes from both having lung-like surface patterns, but they're from entirely different biological kingdoms - one being a lichen and the other a true plant.
compareHints: Tree lungwort is the only Lobaria species commonly found in New England, making it unique in its genus here. Compared to other large foliose lichens in the region, tree lungwort stands out with its distinctive ridged, brain-like surface texture and dramatic color changes when wet. Most similar lichens have smoother surfaces and less pronounced wet-dry color shifts.
